questions.text: What does PostgreSQL use the buffer cache for?

answers.text: To reduce operating-system accesses and disk I/O
To completely replace persistent storage
To store only committed transactions
To perform logical replication without WAL

questions.explanation: The buffer cache smooths out the speed difference between RAM and disk. Once a page is loaded into the cache, PostgreSQL can access it repeatedly without rereading it through the operating system.

questions.text: Which statements about the PostgreSQL buffer cache are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: It is an array of buffers
A buffer contains a data page and additional information about it
The normal data-page size is 8 KB
The size of each page changes automatically depending on the table size

questions.explanation: The lecture describes the buffer cache as an array of buffers containing data pages and service information. The normal page size is 8 KB; it can be changed when PostgreSQL is built.

questions.text: When does a PostgreSQL buffer become “dirty”?

answers.text: When a process modifies data in the page stored in that buffer
Immediately after any page is read from disk
Only after CHECKPOINT is executed
After the page is evicted from the cache

questions.explanation: If the data in a cached page has been modified, the corresponding buffer is dirty and must eventually be written to disk.

questions.text: What happens when a page is evicted from the buffer cache? Select all that apply.

answers.text: A page that has been used less recently than others is selected
If the selected buffer is dirty, its page is written to disk
Another page can be read into the freed buffer
The corresponding table is always deleted during eviction

questions.explanation: The lecture describes an LRU-like principle: a page that has not been used for a long time is selected; a dirty page is written first, after which the buffer can be reused for another page.

questions.text: What problem does write-ahead logging primarily solve?

answers.text: Loss during a crash of changes that still existed only in RAM
Insufficient memory for query sorting
Missing indexes on tables
Object-name conflicts across schemas

questions.explanation: Buffering improves performance, but RAM contents can be lost during a crash. WAL makes it possible to replay the necessary changes and restore a consistent state.

questions.text: Which objects and data are protected by WAL? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Pages of regular tables
Index pages
Transaction status
Temporary-table data

questions.explanation: The lecture states that WAL protects tables, indexes, other WAL-logged objects, and transaction status. Changes to temporary tables are not written to WAL.

questions.text: What is the core principle of write-ahead logging?

answers.text: The WAL record describing a change must reach persistent storage before the changed data page
The data page must always be written before WAL
WAL is created only after a checkpoint completes
All data pages must be written at the same time as WAL

questions.explanation: The ordering “WAL first, changed data later” makes it possible to restore changes after a crash. The documentation defines this as the core idea of WAL.

questions.text: Which statements about WAL are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: A WAL record contains information needed to replay a change
WAL files are stored in PGDATA/pg_wal
Unlogged tables are not protected by WAL
Temporary tables are always fully WAL-logged

questions.explanation: The lecture presents WAL as a stream of information used to replay lost operations; files are stored in pg_wal. Temporary and unlogged tables are excluded from normal WAL protection.

questions.text: What happens to an unlogged table after a crash?

answers.text: It is truncated
It is automatically converted into a temporary table
It is restored exclusively from indexes
It is necessarily dropped together with its schema

questions.explanation: Unlogged tables can be faster because they do not have normal WAL protection, but after a crash their contents are not recovered: the tables are truncated.

questions.text: What happens when PostgreSQL recovers after a crash? Select all that apply.

answers.text: The server enters recovery mode
PostgreSQL reads WAL and replays the required records in order
Recovery begins from the last completed checkpoint
All tables are always reread in full regardless of WAL

questions.explanation: After an abnormal shutdown, the server restores consistency starting from the last completed checkpoint and replaying the necessary WAL records.

questions.text: During recovery, how is a transaction treated if its commit record did not reach WAL before the crash?

answers.text: As aborted
As definitely committed
As read-only
As a prepared two-phase transaction

questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly states that if the commit record did not make it into WAL, the transaction is treated as aborted after the crash.

questions.text: What tasks does a checkpoint perform? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Ensures that all buffers that were dirty at the checkpoint boundary are written to disk
Guarantees that changes made before the checkpoint boundary are present on disk
Limits the amount of WAL needed for crash recovery
Removes all rows belonging to unfinished transactions from the database

questions.explanation: A checkpoint writes the relevant dirty buffers and creates a reference point from which later recovery can begin.

questions.text: When is a checkpoint considered complete?

answers.text: When all buffers that were dirty when the checkpoint began have been written
Immediately after the checkpointer process starts
After the first new WAL file appears
Only after the server is restarted

questions.explanation: The checkpoint position corresponds to the start of writing accumulated dirty buffers, but the checkpoint is complete only after those writes finish.

questions.text: Why can WAL be more efficient than writing changed data pages at every transaction commit? Select all that apply.

answers.text: WAL records are usually smaller than a whole data page
WAL is written sequentially
A single WAL synchronization can confirm several small transactions
WAL completely eliminates the need to ever write data pages

questions.explanation: The documentation emphasizes sequential WAL writes and lower synchronization costs compared with writing many changed data files.

questions.text: What is fsync used for during synchronous commit?

answers.text: To ensure WAL is moved from the operating-system cache to nonvolatile storage
To remove a committed transaction from WAL
To read all table pages into the buffer cache
To force all indexes to be rebuilt

questions.explanation: The lecture explains fsync as necessary to avoid leaving a WAL record only in the OS cache and to ensure that it reaches nonvolatile storage.

questions.text: Which statements about synchronous and asynchronous WAL write modes are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: With synchronous commit, the backend waits for WAL to be written
Asynchronous WAL writing is performed by walwriter
Asynchronous mode improves performance at the cost of a weaker guarantee that a just-acknowledged transaction survives a crash
In asynchronous mode PostgreSQL can no longer restore database consistency after a crash

questions.explanation: Asynchronous writing avoids waiting for an immediate fsync at every commit, but WAL is still used to restore consistency after a crash.

questions.text: How does PostgreSQL obey the WAL rule if a data page must be flushed while the corresponding WAL record is not yet on disk?

answers.text: It first writes the corresponding WAL record synchronously
It flushes the data page and deletes the WAL record
It rolls the entire database back to the previous checkpoint
It ignores WAL if walwriter is running

questions.explanation: Even if WAL records were previously flushed asynchronously, before writing the corresponding data page PostgreSQL must ensure that the required WAL has reached disk.

questions.text: Which mappings between PostgreSQL processes and their tasks are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: walwriter — asynchronous WAL writes to disk
checkpointer — performing checkpoints and flushing the dirty buffers associated with them
bgwriter — background writing of some dirty buffers
bgwriter — mandatory commit processing for every user transaction

questions.explanation: The lecture separates responsibilities: walwriter services WAL, checkpointer performs checkpoints, and the background writer proactively cleans some dirty buffers that are likely to be evicted.

questions.text: Why does the background writer proactively write some dirty buffers?

answers.text: To reduce the chance that a backend must wait for a dirty buffer to be written during eviction
To replace walwriter
To prevent pages from being evicted from the cache
To perform logical decoding of WAL

questions.explanation: Bgwriter tries to write buffers that are likely to be evicted soon, reducing backend latency.

questions.text: Which statements about wal_level values are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: minimal contains enough information for crash recovery
replica adds information needed for backup and replication
logical adds information needed to obtain logical row changes
minimal is intended for logical replication of row changes

questions.explanation: The material lists minimal, replica, and logical with increasing amounts of WAL information and corresponding additional capabilities.

questions.text: Which wal_level is used by default?

answers.text: replica
minimal
logical
archive

questions.explanation: The WAL-level slide identifies replica as the default level.

questions.text: What happens when PostgreSQL is stopped in fast mode? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Open connections are terminated
A checkpoint is performed before shutdown
Consistent data is written to disk, so the next startup does not require crash recovery
The server deliberately leaves data in a state similar to a hardware crash

questions.explanation: In fast mode, the server terminates connections and performs a checkpoint. Shutdown may take longer, but crash recovery is not required at the next startup.

questions.text: How does an immediate PostgreSQL shutdown fundamentally differ from a fast shutdown?

answers.text: Immediate shutdown does not perform a checkpoint before stopping, so startup requires WAL recovery
Immediate shutdown always waits for all client transactions to finish
Immediate shutdown completely deletes WAL
Immediate shutdown automatically switches wal_level to logical

questions.explanation: Immediate mode stops the server without a checkpoint. The on-disk state is similar to a crash, and PostgreSQL restores consistency from WAL at the next startup.

questions.text: What additional capabilities does WAL provide besides recovery from an ordinary crash? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Creating physical backups without requiring an instantaneous snapshot of every file
Point-in-time recovery to a moment available in retained WAL data
Supporting replication between servers
Automatically fixing any user logical error without a backup

questions.explanation: The documentation connects WAL not only with REDO after a crash but also with physical backup and point-in-time recovery. The lecture additionally emphasizes WAL as the basis for replication.
